subject: English
topic: Tenses — Fill in the Blank and Error Spotting (Set W7)

questions.stem: Yesterday, I _____ to the market early in the morning.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Yesterday' signals a completed past action → simple past tense. 'Went' is the simple past of 'go'. 'Have gone' (present perfect) cannot be used with specific past time words like 'yesterday'. 'Was going' (past continuous) implies an ongoing action that was interrupted — not indicated here.

questions.stem: She _____ here since 2019, and she loves the city.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Since 2019' + she still lives there → present perfect continuous: has/have + been + V-ing. 'Has been living' indicates an ongoing action from a point in the past up to now. 'Had been living' would require a past reference point. Simple past 'lived' suggests it ended, which contradicts 'loves the city' (present).

questions.stem: The sun _____ in the east and _____ in the west — this is a permanent scientific fact.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Universal truths, scientific facts, and habits use simple present tense. 'Rises' and 'sets' are correct. Past tense (rose/set) refers to a specific past event. Present perfect/continuous are wrong for permanent truths. Rule: universal facts → always simple present.

questions.stem: By the time the ambulance arrived, the patient _____ consciousness.
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'By the time X happened (past), Y had already happened (earlier past)' → past perfect. The consciousness was lost BEFORE the ambulance arrived. Structure: By the time + simple past → past perfect in the main clause. 'Had already lost' is correct.

questions.stem: If the prices _____ any higher, we will have to cut down on expenses.
questions.explanation: B is correct. In Type 1 conditional (real/likely condition), the structure is: If + simple present → will + base form. 'If prices rise..., we will have to cut expenses.' Option D ('will rise') is a common error — the 'if' clause never uses 'will' in standard English conditionals.

questions.stem: I _____ him for years before I finally recognised him at the airport.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Before I finally recognised him' = past event. The period of not seeing him happened BEFORE recognising him → past perfect negative: 'hadn't seen'. 'Didn't see' (simple past) implies a single event, not a duration. 'Haven't seen' is present perfect — wrong tense for a completed past situation.

questions.stem: She _____ a novel when the power suddenly went off.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Was V-ing ... when ...' is the classic pattern for a longer ongoing past action interrupted by a sudden event. 'She was writing' (past continuous) when the power 'went off' (simple past, the interruption). Past perfect ('had written') would suggest the writing was fully completed before the power went off.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatical error in: 'She has been worked here for the past ten years.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Has been worked' is wrong — the present perfect continuous requires: has/have + been + V-ing (present participle). The correct form is 'has been working'. 'Worked' (past participle) creates a passive structure ('has been worked' = is worked on by someone), which changes the meaning completely. Fix: 'She has been working here for ten years.'

questions.stem: By 2035, scientists _____ a cure for the most common form of cancer.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Future perfect (will have + V3) is used for an action that WILL BE COMPLETED before a specific future point in time. 'By 2035' signals the deadline. Pattern: 'By [future time], subject + will have + V3.' 'Will develop' (simple future) doesn't emphasise completion before the deadline.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly reported speech form of: He said, 'I am going to the market.'

options.option_text: He said that he is going to the market.
He told that he was going to the market.
He said that he was going to the market.
He said that he will go to the market.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Indirect speech rules: 'said' (past reporting verb) triggers tense backshift. 'am going' (present continuous) → 'was going' (past continuous). Option A fails to backshift tense. Option B uses 'told' without an object — 'told' requires a person ('told me/him...'). Option D changes meaning from continuous to simple.
